source.title: LLM Circuit Analyses Are Consistent Across Training and Scale
source.authors: Curt Tigges; Michael Hanna; Qi-Nan Yu; Stella Biderman

record.tranche_reason: The study measures induction-head behavior over training checkpoints using a prefix-matching-based induction score, following the original measurement, on Pythia models at several scales. It does not reproduce the original in-context-learning loss analysis.
record.gate_note: The study scores induction-head behavior over training and reports its timing relative to Greater-Than task performance. It does not measure loss by token index, the in-context-learning gain in the claim, or a bump in the training loss curve. The reported IOI and Greater-Than task-performance outcomes are not themselves in-context-learning measurements.
record.test_reason: The study scores induction behaviour with Olsson et al.'s prefix-matching score across Pythia checkpoints, 70M–2.8B. It reports when induction heads emerge across scales, which bears on V4 and on the timing part of V2. It does not measure in-context learning, loss by token index or a loss bump. It does not test mechanism in small attention-only models.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors also conclude that circuit algorithms (IOI) stay stable over training and across scales even as individual heads change, and that circuit size correlates with model size. Results are limited to simple tasks and one model family.
record.recipe_differences: Uses a prefix-matching-based induction-head score over Pythia checkpoints, but does not reproduce the original in-context-learning loss-by-token analysis or its loss-curve result.

fits_no_version.finding: In Pythia-160m, individual heads gain and later lose induction behaviour over 300B tokens, while other heads take their place and task performance stays stable.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: The identity of the heads showing induction behaviour shifts during long training, while the overall induction function persists.

fits_no_version.finding: Greater-Than performance emerges immediately after induction heads emerge.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In Pythia models, induction-head emergence slightly precedes Greater-Than task ability.

record.problems: Induction-score outcomes are primarily shown in figures, with no model-specific textual account of each trajectory. The study analyzes only Pythia, omits 6.9B and 12B models from circuit finding, and does not measure in-context learning by token-index loss or the proposed loss bump.

untested.parts: All parts. There is no test of composition with a previous-token head via the prefix-matching score, and no small attention-only models.
Abruptness is not quantified. Coincidence with an in-context-learning gain and a loss-curve bump is not measured.
Other model families, separate training runs with the same configuration, other architectures and modalities. Pythia 6.9B and 12B are excluded from circuit and component analysis.

missing.what: Per-head induction scores over training for the top heads in Pythia-160m (head turnover).

The Pythia-160m IOI circuit diagram shows a previous-token head (2.6) feeding induction heads (4.11, 4.6, 5.0), with the induction/duplicate-token edge share over training. This bears on the composition structure, but in a non-attention-only model and without a direct composition test.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V4 limits_scope label was removed, because confinement to one family is an untested part, not a qualifying result. The V1 supports label was removed, because the attention-pattern score cannot show composition and the models are not attention-only. The induction score is restricted to Greater-Than circuit heads and normalised per model, so absolute strength across models cannot be compared.

versions.untested_parts: The study measures induction behavior but does not test whether it is implemented by composing with an earlier previous-token head, nor does it use small attention-only transformers.
Only Pythia models from 70M to 2.8B parameters are included in circuit finding; the study does not test other model families, separate training runs, other architectures, or modalities.

relation.reason: Its own induction-score measurements bear on emergence timing and occurrence across model sizes.

tranche.reason: Reports induction-attention emergence across Pythia scales and checkpoints in task circuits, a new setting; it does not reproduce the original ICL and loss-curve analysis.

source_check.notes: Section 3.2 describes summing scores over in-circuit heads and normalizing across checkpoints, whereas Section 4.1 retrospectively describes Figure 2 as plotting the top component; this reporting inconsistency does not alter the textual timing result. The authors' conclusion paraphrase matches the abstract and discussion.

statements.correction: Pythia 70M–2.8B; 300B training tokens; most models' induction heads emerge soon after 2 × 10^9 tokens; Greater-Than behavior follows immediately. Figure 2 uses induction scores summed over in-circuit heads and normalized across checkpoints. Appendix D: prefix-matching attention scores on repeated segments. No ICL loss-by-position or loss-bump measurement.
statements.problem: The timing and model-size numbers are correct, but the shared framing overstates what this study establishes: the text reports emergence in most models without quantifying abruptness or transition width. Appendix D specifies repeated segments but does not state that their tokens are random; the supplied text also does not identify the training corpus as the Pile.
